_note: How NASA's Mission Design Lab decides whether a design is real. The MDL is part of Goddard's Integrated Design Center: a room of subsystem engineers who size a mission concept together in about a week. They never sign off on the numbers an engineer first writes down - they add a contingency to every one, then check the design still fits. These are those contingencies.
_source: Karpati, G., Hyde, T., Peabody, H., Garrison, M., 'Resource Management and Contingencies in Aerospace Concurrent Engineering', NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, 2012. NTRS 20120013284. Section on the discipline-by-discipline contingency and margin policies in use at the IDC.
lab: Mission Design Lab, Integrated Design Center, NASA Goddard
_definitionsNote: The three numbers every subsystem reports. The whole method is the gap between them: you design with MEV, not CBE, because parts always get heavier than the first guess.

definitions.name: Current Best Estimate
definitions.plain: What we think it weighs, draws or sends today.
definitions.detail: The honest number from the engineer who owns that box, with nothing added for safety.

definitions.name: Maximum Expected Value
definitions.plain: What it could realistically grow to before it launches.
definitions.detail: CBE plus a contingency. Real parts almost always get heavier and hungrier between the first drawing and the launch pad, so this is the number a careful engineer actually designs to.

definitions.name: Maximum Possible Value
definitions.plain: The hard limit. The rocket, the panels or the dish cannot go past this.
definitions.detail: Set by the hardware you picked, not by opinion. If MEV goes past MPV the design does not close and something has to change.

_formulaNote: Straight out of the paper, which argues that the bare words 'contingency' and 'margin' cause real confusion and should always be qualified.

formulas.label: Growth contingency
formulas.plain: How much room for growth you added, measured against today's estimate.

formulas.label: Resource contingency
formulas.plain: The same room, measured against the grown number instead.

formulas.label: Growth margin
formulas.plain: How much spare you still have above the grown number.

formulas.label: Resource margin
formulas.plain: The same spare, measured against the hard limit.

_contingencyNote: The percentages the IDC actually adds, by subsystem. Each one is quoted from the paper in `quote`, so nothing here is invented.

contingencies.label: Dry mass
contingencies.appliesTo: Everything that is not fuel: the bus, the instruments, the panels, the dish, the engine.
contingencies.quote: 25% contingency is carried over the CBE mass of an avionics box.
contingencies.plain: Add a quarter to the weight. Parts always come in heavier than the drawing.

contingencies.label: Power
contingencies.appliesTo: Every instrument, the radio and the engine, added up.
contingencies.quote: the power delivered have a minimum of 30% contingency over the total CBE loads
contingencies.plain: The panels must make a third more than everything on board asks for.

contingencies.label: Data rate
contingencies.appliesTo: The science data the instruments produce.
contingencies.quote: The RF Comm subsystem gets the CBE data rate from Science, and adds 30% contingency to it.
contingencies.plain: Assume the instruments make a third more data than they promised.

contingencies.label: Delta-v (ACS tax)
contingencies.appliesTo: The speed change the whole trip needs.
contingencies.quote: Add 5 % ACS Tax on all delta-v numbers.
contingencies.plain: Pointing and steering burn fuel too. The paper calls this a tax, because every mission pays it.

contingencies.label: Propellant residuals
contingencies.quote: Add 3% to 5% for ullage and residuals on total propellant
contingencies.plain: You can never use the last drop in the tank. Some fuel is always left clinging inside.

_pileUpNote: The paper's sharpest warning, and the reason a design can fail review even when every single subsystem followed the rules. Each engineer adds their own contingency to a number that already had one added. The game shows this as the composite contingency.

pileUp.title: Contingency pile-up
pileUp.quote: concurrent design products are vulnerable to contingency pile-ups, especially so to hidden contingency pile-ups
pileUp.plain: Every team adds their own safety margin on top of a number that already had one. Do it four times and the spacecraft is far heavier than anybody intended.
pileUp.example: Science says it makes 10 kbps. Comms adds 30% and picks a bigger radio. That radio draws more power, so Power adds 30% on top and fits bigger panels. Bigger panels weigh more, so Mechanical adds 25% and fits stronger struts. Nobody broke a rule, and the spacecraft doubled.

_verdictNote: What the review says at the end. A design that closes on CBE but not on MEV is the interesting case: it is the one that looks fine and is not.

verdicts.label: Design closes
verdicts.plain: Every subsystem fits even after NASA's contingency is added. The Mission Design Lab would sign this off.

verdicts.label: Closes, but tight
verdicts.plain: It fits, but with almost nothing spare. A real review would ask you to find more margin before Phase A.

verdicts.label: Does not close
verdicts.plain: It fits on paper but not once contingency is added. This is exactly the design a review exists to catch.

_marginNote: The spare a project manager is expected to still be holding when the concept study ends. Goddard's own figure.
expectedMarginSource: Di Pietro, D., NASA Goddard: the project manager at the start of Phase B holds 25% margins for power and dry mass resources.
_toneNote: Thresholds for the colour of each row. Resource margin above comfortable is green, above tight is amber, below zero is red.
